props.title: Armageddon
props.initialSlug: Oil drillers race to save Earth from killer asteroid

sections.content: Armageddon (1998) epitomizes Michael Bay's bombastic blockbuster style - a testosterone-fueled disaster film that launched a wave of late-90s asteroid destruction movies. Coming out the same summer as Deep Impact (1998), it took a more action-heavy approach to Earth-threatening space objects. The film established Bay's signature rapid-cut editing style, orange-tinted explosions, and heroic low-angle shots that would define blockbuster aesthetics for years to come. While critically panned, it remains a masterclass in crowd-pleasing spectacle, with Bruce Willis leading a crew of deep-core drillers turned astronauts in a mission to save Earth.

sections.content: The film sits at a crucial intersection of practical and CGI effects, marking a transition point in how Hollywood approached large-scale disaster sequences. While Twister (1996) and Independence Day (1996) had already pushed CGI boundaries, Armageddon's $140 million budget allowed for unprecedented scale in its space sequences. The film's influence can be seen in later disaster epics like 2012 (2009) and San Andreas (2015), though few matched its combination of practical explosions and early CGI.

The film's emotional core - despite its over-the-top action - centers on the father-daughter relationship between Willis and Liv Tyler, backed by Aerosmith's "I Don't Want to Miss a Thing." This formula of combining spectacular destruction with personal stakes would become standard for disaster films like The Day After Tomorrow (2004) and Greenland (2020). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: Armageddon's impact on blockbuster filmmaking extends beyond just disaster movies. Its rapid editing style, with average shot lengths under 2 seconds, influenced action cinematography in films like Transformers (2007) and Battle: Los Angeles (2011). The film's mix of humor and apocalyptic stakes created a template followed by later sci-fi adventures like Don't Look Up (2021).
